Sunlight looks white, right? Actually, that’s an optical illusion! Sunlight is really made up of all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. 

Light travels through space in waves. Some colors, like red and orange, travel in long, lazy waves. Others, like blue and violet, travel in short, choppy waves. 

Sunlight flies in a straight line until it hits Earth’s atmosphere, which is a thick blanket of gases—mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Imagine the atmosphere as a giant pinball machine. The long, lazy red waves easily glide right past the gas molecules without hitting much. 

However, the short, choppy blue waves crash directly into these tiny gas molecules and bounce around in every direction. Scientists call this **Rayleigh scattering**. Because blue light gets scattered all over the place, when you look up on a clear day, that’s the color bouncing into your eyes!

Wait—if violet waves are even shorter than blue, why isn’t the sky purple? Two reasons: first, the sun naturally sends out way more blue light than violet. Second, human eyes are much better at detecting blue. So, thanks to bouncing light waves and the way your eyes work, we get a brilliant blue sky!

Imagine baking a cake. The first time, you have to go to the store to buy every single ingredient, which takes a while. The second time, you already have flour, sugar, and spices in your pantry, so you only need to buy fresh milk and eggs. Much faster! 

Your web browser’s **cache** (pronounced "cash") works just like that pantry. 

Every website is built from lots of individual files, including images, logos, fonts, and layout instructions. The first time you visit a site, your browser has to download all these pieces over the internet. 

To save time later, your browser stores copies of the unchanging parts—like a site's logo or background—in a temporary storage folder on your computer or phone. That folder is the cache. 

The next time you visit that website, your browser doesn't have to download everything from scratch. It instantly grabs the saved files right from your device's cache and only downloads brand-new content. This makes your favorite websites load much faster and uses less internet data. 

Occasionally, a website updates, and your browser accidentally loads outdated files from your "pantry," making the site look broken. That’s why tech support sometimes tells you to "clear your cache"—it forces your browser to fetch fresh ingredients!

Imagine you want to bake cookies, so you go to the store to buy flour, sugar, and chocolate chips. If you decide to bake again tomorrow, you do not go back to the store for flour because you already have the rest of the bag in your pantry. A browser cache works just like that pantry, except it stores website ingredients on your computer or phone.

To save time later, your browser quietly saves copies of these heavy, unchanging files into a temporary storage folder on your device called the cache.

The next time you visit that same website, your browser checks its cache first. Instead of downloading the logos and fonts from the internet all over again, it instantly loads them directly from your device. It only uses the internet to fetch brand new updates, like today's news headlines. This clever shortcut makes your favorite websites load much faster and saves your internet data.

The Atlantic always spat things up after a gale: splintered lobster traps, tangled kelp, sea glass smoothed by a century of churning. After thirty years tending the beacon at Gull’s Tooth, Arthur thought he had cataloged every brand of maritime debris.

Then he heard the ringing.

At first, he blamed the wind whistling through the rusted railings. Yet as he descended the slick basalt steps toward the tide line, the sound sharpened. It wasn't the shriek of a gull or the groan of shifting timber. It was a bright, synthetic marimba tune, cheerfully repeating against the roar of the surf.

Arthur squinted through the salt spray, his heavy boots crunching over barnacles. Twelve miles of grey water separated this rock from the mainland, and cellular signals never reached the reef.

Wedged between two black boulders, half submerged in a frothy tide pool, a rectangular screen pulsed with pale blue light.

Arthur knelt, his knees popping in the damp cold. Freezing seawater lapped directly over the spiderwebbed glass, yet the tiny speaker persisted, shrill and impossibly demanding. Through a sheen of cold Atlantic brine, the glowing display illuminated a trembling green icon below a single, impossible caller ID: *THE LANTERN ROOM*.

The morning after the gale, Arthur walked the jagged perimeter of Blackwake Island to see what the Atlantic had surrendered. Usually, the tide left tangled lobster traps, bleached driftwood, and translucent jellyfish glistening on the dark basalt. Today, it left a sound that did not belong to the sea.

Beneath the rhythmic thunder of the surf and the harsh cries of wheeling gulls, a bright, synthetic melody chimed through the mist. Arthur paused, tightening the collar of his heavy oilskin coat against the salt spray. No boats had passed the headland in three weeks. He lived entirely alone beneath the sweeping, mechanical eye of the lighthouse.

He picked his way carefully across the slick kelp, his rubber boots crunching loudly on pale barnacles. The music stopped, leaving only the cold hiss of receding foam, then started again with stubborn urgency.

Wedged tightly between two wet boulders lay a sleek black smartphone. Its glass screen glowed fiercely in the gray dawn, entirely uncracked despite the brutal teeth of the shoreline. Raindrops beaded across the illuminated display, distorting the single word flashing at its center: HOME.

Arthur knelt beside the freezing tide pool, reaching a trembling, weathered hand toward the impossible call.

Today marks one year since I transitioned from Individual Contributor to Engineering Manager. 

People told me before I started: "Management isn’t a promotion; it’s a career change." They couldn't have been more right. Trading my IDE for 1:1s and strategy docs was jarring at first, and the learning curve has been steep.

🔹 **Redefine productivity:** Walking away from the code felt like losing my superpower. I had to stop measuring my worth by PRs merged and start measuring it by how effectively I unblock and empower my team. 

🔹 **Listen more, solve less:** My engineer brain desperately wants to jump in and fix every problem. Stepping back to ask guiding questions instead of giving answers builds trust, autonomy, and a much stronger team.

🔹 **Protect the shield, share the context:** My job isn't to micromanage tasks; it’s to absorb organizational chaos while clearly translating the *why* behind our work.

Set in the roaring 1920s, F. Scott Fitzgerald’s *The Great Gatsby* follows Nick Carraway, who moves to Long Island next door to the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. Gatsby throws extravagant parties hoping to attract his lost love, Nick’s cousin Daisy, who lives across the bay with her wealthy, unfaithful husband, Tom Buchanan. Nick reunites the former lovers, reigniting their affair. However, tensions peak during a confrontation in Manhattan, and on the drive home, Daisy accidentally strikes and kills Tom’s mistress with Gatsby’s car. Gatsby takes the blame to protect Daisy, prompting the mistress’s grieving husband to murder Gatsby before taking his own life. Callously, Tom and Daisy retreat into their privileged lives, leaving Nick completely disillusioned.

At its core, the novel serves as a poignant critique of the American Dream, illustrating how the pursuit of happiness and self-invention has been corrupted by materialism and greed. Fitzgerald also highlights the rigid barriers of social class; despite Gatsby’s immense "new money," he can never truly penetrate the exclusive, careless world of Tom and Daisy’s "old money." Ultimately, through Gatsby's obsession, the novel explores the illusion of recapturing the past, proving that chasing idealized memories leads only to tragedy.

Finally, Gatsby’s tragic obsession underscores the impossibility of recapturing the past, proving that time cannot be rewritten by willpower alone.

Johannes Gutenberg’s invention of the movable-type printing press around 1440 sparked an information revolution that fundamentally transformed Europe. Before its arrival, books were painstakingly hand-copied by scribes, making them rare, expensive, and accessible only to the wealthy elite and the clergy. The printing press allowed for the rapid, cheap mass production of texts, democratizing knowledge on an unprecedented scale.

This surge in affordable reading material dramatically increased literacy rates across the continent and encouraged printing in everyday vernacular languages rather than exclusively in Latin. This linguistic shift standardized national languages and fostered distinct cultural identities. 

Crucially, the press fueled three monumental movements that shaped modern Europe. First, it accelerated the Renaissance by preserving and spreading classical Greek and Roman texts. Second, it ignited the Protestant Reformation; Martin Luther’s *Ninety-five Theses* and vernacular translations of the Bible spread rapidly, shattering the Catholic Church’s monopoly on religious truth. Finally, it powered the Scientific Revolution by allowing researchers to accurately share data, diagrams, and discoveries, enabling collaborative progress across borders.

Ultimately, by breaking the institutional stranglehold on information, the printing press empowered the individual, encouraged critical thinking, and laid the intellectual foundations for the modern world.

By making information accessible to the general public, the printing press pulled Europe out of the Middle Ages and forged the modern world.

If you have an evening to spare, Kuro Ramen serves a bowl of tonkotsu that borders on spiritual. The broth is an absolute masterpiece: velvety, rich, and clearly simmered for days. Each spoonful delivers a deep, savory punch of pork, garlic, and umami that coats the springy noodles perfectly. Topped with tender chashu and a jammy egg, the food rivals Tokyo’s finest. 

Unfortunately, your patience will be tested before that first glorious slurp. The service is glacially slow. After being seated, we waited twenty minutes just for water, and nearly fifty minutes for our ramen to arrive. Flagging down a server for the check felt nearly impossible. The staff is polite, just visibly overwhelmed and severely understaffed.

Still, the culinary payoff is undeniable. Visit Kuro Ramen for the transcendent, comforting broth, not for a quick weeknight bite. Bring good company to pass the time, and prepare to wait. Four stars.

Flagging down a server for the check felt nearly impossible despite the dining room being only half full.

Visit for the unforgettable broth, but clear your entire afternoon schedule before you sit down.

While remote work offers undeniable flexibility, a fully remote environment ultimately hurts junior engineers during the most critical phase of their career development. Early-career software engineering is as much an apprenticeship as it is a technical job, relying heavily on osmotic learning that simply vanishes behind a screen. In a physical office, juniors absorb invaluable tacit knowledge by overhearing senior developers debate architecture, watching a mentor navigate a tricky terminal command, or jumping into spontaneous whiteboard sessions. Remote work replaces this frictionless collaboration with scheduled Zoom calls and formal Slack messages. For a junior already battling imposter syndrome, typing out a formal request for help feels far more intimidating than tapping a neighbor on the shoulder, often resulting in hours of isolated wheel-spinning over minor bugs. Furthermore, building professional networks and grasping company culture is significantly harder from a bedroom desk, stalling crucial soft-skill development and reducing visibility for future promotions. Although disciplined teams can mitigate these issues through hyper-intentional pair programming and structured documentation, most fast-paced tech companies struggle to maintain that rigor consistently. Ultimately, trading short-term convenience for long-term mentorship leaves remote junior engineers at a distinct disadvantage compared to their in-office peers when building foundational skills.

While remote work offers undeniable flexibility for seasoned industry veterans, it fundamentally hurts junior engineers during the most critical phase of their careers. Early career software development relies heavily on learning through osmosis, a process that digital communication simply cannot replicate. In a physical office, novices overhear senior engineers debating system architecture, absorb unwritten cultural and technical team norms, and easily ask quick clarifying questions by turning to a desk mate. Conversely, in a remote environment, seeking assistance requires scheduling a formal video call or sending an intrusive chat message. This artificial barrier often breeds imposter syndrome, causing juniors to struggle in isolation for hours over trivial bugs rather than risk bothering a busy colleague. Furthermore, remote code reviews can feel sterile and overly critical without the softening context of personal rapport. Mentorship thrives on spontaneous interactions, whiteboard sessions, and shared daily frustrations, all of which vanish behind a solitary glowing computer screen. Although working from home eliminates exhausting commutes and allows for deep focus, beginners rarely lack focus; they lack direction and tacit knowledge. Ultimately, trading collaborative immersion for domestic convenience stunts professional growth, leaving new developers technically isolated precisely when they need community and immediate guidance the most.

Both running and swimming are powerhouse cardiovascular exercises that boost heart health, burn significant calories, and reduce stress. However, they offer distinct physical benefits and practical trade-offs.

Running’s greatest strength is accessibility. With just a pair of supportive shoes, you can work out almost anywhere, anytime. As a weight-bearing activity, it increases bone density and builds strong lower-body muscles. Its main drawback is high impact; repetitive pounding on pavement stresses the knees, hips, and ankles, raising the risk of overuse injuries.

Conversely, swimming is virtually zero-impact. Water’s buoyancy supports your body, making it ideal for people with arthritis, joint pain, or injuries. Furthermore, swimming provides a superior full-body workout, toning the upper body, core, and legs simultaneously against natural water resistance, while also boosting lung capacity through controlled breathing. Its primary limitation is convenience, as it requires access to a pool or safe open water, plus extra gear like swimwear and goggles.

Ultimately, the better option depends on your body and lifestyle. Running offers unmatched convenience and bone-strengthening power, while swimming delivers a gentle, comprehensive workout that spares your joints. For optimal fitness, combining both creates a well-rounded, sustainable routine.

Running and swimming are two of the most effective cardiovascular exercises for staying fit, yet they offer distinctly different physical benefits and challenges.

Running is unmatched in its convenience. Requiring only a supportive pair of shoes, you can exercise almost anywhere. Because it is a weight-bearing activity, running increases bone density and builds strong leg muscles while burning calories rapidly. However, repetitive pounding on hard surfaces makes it a high-impact sport, which can strain joints and cause knee or ankle injuries over time.

Conversely, swimming provides a comprehensive workout without the harsh physical toll. Water buoyancy supports your weight, making swimming an ideal low-impact option for people with joint pain or mobility issues. Moving against water resistance engages your arms, shoulders, core, and legs simultaneously, building balanced muscle tone and lung capacity. Its primary drawback is logistics, since you need access to a pool or safe open water.

Ultimately, the best choice depends on your body and lifestyle. Running offers simplicity and bone-building power, while swimming delivers gentle, total-body conditioning. Incorporating either activity into your weekly routine, or combining both for variety, will significantly boost your overall cardiovascular health, stamina, and mental well-being.

**1/5**
Junior devs write simple code because they have to. 
Mid-level devs write clever code because they can. 
Senior devs write simple code because they know better.

Here is why "boring" code beats clever code every single time: 🧵👇

**2/5**
Code is read 10x more than it is written. 

That nested, regex-heavy one-liner might save you 5 lines of code today, but it costs your teammates 15 minutes of mental gymnastics tomorrow. 

Optimize for human readability, not line count. The compiler doesn't care how smart you look.

**3/5**
Remember Kernighan’s Law: "Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place."

If you write code at the absolute limit of your cleverness, you are—by definition—not smart enough to debug it. Especially not when production goes down at 3 AM.

**4/5**
Software is a team sport. 

Clever code is usually driven by ego ("Look at this trick I know"). 
Simple code is driven by empathy ("Let me make this easy for the next person").

Spoiler alert: 6 months from now, when you've forgotten all the context, that "next person" is you.

**5/5**
Anyone can make a simple problem look complex. True mastery is making a complex problem look boringly simple. 

Drop the magic. Write obvious code. Your team (and future you) will thank you.

1/5

Early in my career, I loved cramming complex logic into a single line. Now, I try to write the most boring, obvious code possible. 

Here is why simple code always wins: 🧵

2/5
Code is read far more often than it is written. 

You write a function once, but your team will read it dozens of times over the next few years. Always optimize for the reader's mental energy, not the writer's typing speed.

3/5
Debugging is twice as hard as writing code in the first place. 

If you write the most clever code you are capable of, you are by definition not smart enough to debug it when production breaks at 2 AM. Simple logic leaves nowhere for bugs to hide.

4/5
Simple code scales your engineering team. 

When logic is straightforward, new hires onboard faster and code reviews take minutes instead of hours. Cleverness creates knowledge silos where only the original author can fix things.

5/5
Future you is a complete stranger. 

In six months, you will have zero memory of why you used an obscure language trick today. Be kind to your future self. Leave your ego out of the editor and write code that anyone can understand.
